title: Training Agents to Fail Predictably: Fine-Tuning for Forecastable Tail Risk
claim: Training the model on forecast error over simulated deployment splits reshapes its risk tail, so extrapolated worst-case forecasts become accurate.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; bar charts with extrapolation line and gradient arrows
description: Three panels, (a) to (c), left to right. Panel (a) shows a row of circles for tasks, with fit-set tasks in orange and deployment tasks in gray. Lines run from the circles through a model θ box to a bar chart of risk scores. A pink arrow reads 'train θ to reduce forecast error'. A 'risk scores sorted' arrow leads to panel (b). Panel (b) shows sorted bars with a green-to-red risk gradient, the top-k fit bars in orange, and a dashed orange line extrapolated to a 'forecast' circle. A navy 'actual' dot sits above it, and the gap is labeled 'forecast error' in red. Green arrows mark gradients that are kept, and red ✗ marks gradients that are masked. Panel (c) stacks two small plots. Plain safety training leaves a visible error. 'Ours' lands on the actual point, marked with a green check.
caption: Fine-tuning a model for accurate forecasts of its tail risk. (a) A risk score measures how close the model comes to failure on each task. At test time, we forecast the worst case in deployment from a small fit set of new tasks. To train for this, we split each training task set at random into a small fit set and a large deployment set, so called because it simulates deployment. (b) Following [ref], we fit a line to the top $k$ fit scores and extrapolate it to rarer tasks. We train the model to reduce the line's errors on the deployment set (red), passing each score's gradient (arrows) only when following it would lower that task's risk score, and we add a regularizer to preserve the primary behavior. (c) Safety training that lowers every score by the same factor does not change the tail's shape, so the forecast may still under-predict the worst case (top). Our training changes the shape, so that on new tasks, a forecast from the fit set alone is accurate (bottom).
abstract: Before deployment, an AI system might be evaluated on thousands or even millions of inputs, but after deployment it may encounter billions, so its worst failures may not appear during evaluation. Jones et al. (2025) proposed forecasting how risky the riskiest deployment inputs will be by scoring how close the system comes to failure on each evaluation input and extrapolating from the highest scores. We show that the error of this forecast splits into a noise term, whose distribution is the same for every model up to scale, and terms that depend on the shape of the tail of the model's risk scores. These model-dependent terms can make the forecast under-predict badly, both in theory, whenever the evaluation set lacks a rare kind of input that deployment contains, and in practice: on real user prompts marked as toxic, the forecast under-predicted the probability that a response begins with an offensive word for all eleven language models we tested. Because the shape of this tail is a property of the model, we propose fine-tuning the model itself to make the forecast accurate, using the forecast error as the training loss. In a model organism of jailbreaking and in an RL gridworld with rare traps, our method reduced the held-out squared forecast error by factors of 14 to 60, lowered worst-case risk about as much as direct risk minimization (or more), and preserved the model's primary behavior. For settings in which the model should change as little as possible, we show that training with an alternative safety constraint and an added loss term improved the forecast with far smaller changes to the model. Our method also improved the forecast in RL from sampled returns, in language models of up to 8B parameters, and (with minimal-change training) on the toxic user prompts.
